prompt: `ng new` stopped with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'edgesOut')`. What was wrong?

choices.text: A file `ng new` wrote had a syntax error that npm could not read
choices.why: Every file was written, and nothing in them was read by the step that broke.

choices.text: A defect in npm 10.9.4 itself
choices.why: Right. It trips over a chain of optional peer dependencies; npm 11 does not.

choices.text: The registry was unreachable, and npm reported it badly
choices.why: A network failure has its own codes, `ECONNREFUSED` and the like, and the package list had already been fetched.

choices.text: Angular 21 does not support npm, only pnpm
choices.why: The project's own `packageManager` field names npm.

prompt: `legacy-peer-deps=true` stops npm from installing peer dependencies on its own. Why is that safe for this project?

choices.text: Peer dependencies are only used by tests, never by the application
choices.why: Some are needed at run time; the point is that this project lists them.

choices.text: npm 10.9.4 does not support peer dependencies at all
choices.why: It does; it crashed while resolving them.

choices.text: Because `save-exact` installs the peers in their place
choices.why: `save-exact` decides how a version is written down, not what is installed.

choices.text: Every package the project needs is already named in its `package.json`
choices.why: Right. With nothing left for npm to add, the setting only skips the step that crashes.

prompt: In `package.json`, what does `"@angular/core": "^21.2.0"` allow that `"21.2.25"` does not?

choices.text: Any newer 21
choices.why: Right. Two installs a week apart can then get different code.

choices.text: Any older version, down to 21.0.0, if the newer one fails to install
choices.why: npm never falls back to an older version.

choices.text: Version 22, once it is released
choices.why: The caret stops before the next major.

choices.text: Nothing: npm treats the two the same since version 7
choices.why: They are different ranges, and npm treats them differently.

prompt: A colleague clones the planner on a second computer. Which command gives them exactly the `node_modules` you have?

choices.text: `npm install`, which reads `package.json` and takes the newest that matches
choices.why: With exact versions in `package.json` it would take those, but the packages they brought in would still be chosen that day.

choices.text: `npm ci`, which rebuilds it from `package-lock.json`
choices.why: Right. The lockfile names every package, direct or not.

choices.text: `npx ng new planner`, run again in the same folder
choices.why: That would write a new project over the old one.

choices.text: `git clone` alone, since `node_modules` is in the repository
choices.why: `.gitignore` leaves `node_modules` out of the repository.

prompt: How many megabytes did `du -sh node_modules` report for the new project?
Match each file with what it is for.

pairs.right: what `ng build`, `ng serve` and `ng test` do
the first code that runs, which starts the application
the providers the application can be given
the one page the browser asks for

right_distractors: the list of addresses the router knows

prompt: `src/index.html` contains `<app-root></app-root>`. Where does the name `app-root` come from?

choices.text: It is an HTML element every browser knows
choices.why: Browsers know no such element; it means nothing until Angular draws there.

choices.text: From `angular.json`, which names the page's root element
choices.why: `angular.json` names files and builders, not elements.

choices.text: The `selector` of the root component, `App`
choices.why: Right. `bootstrapApplication(App, ...)` draws `App` where its selector appears.

choices.text: From the project's name, `planner`, with the prefix added
choices.why: That would be `app-planner`; the name is the selector's.

prompt: A page stays blank in the browser, and the terminal shows a successful build. Which file's code would have told you why, and where?

choices.text: `src/main.ts`, whose `catch` prints the error in the browser's console
choices.why: Right. A build can succeed and the start still fail; the console is the first place to look.

choices.text: `angular.json`, which writes start-up errors to the dev server's terminal
choices.why: The dev server reports build errors; a failure in the browser is reported in the browser.

choices.text: `app.spec.ts`, whose second test fails when the page is blank
choices.why: A test runs in jsdom when you run `ng test`, not when a page opens.

choices.text: `src/index.html`, which shows a message inside `<app-root>`
choices.why: It shows nothing there; the element is empty until Angular draws.

prompt: You save `public/courses.json` while `ng serve` is running, and `curl` on `/courses.json` returns the start of `index.html`. Why?

choices.text: The JSON has a syntax error, so the server sends the page instead
choices.why: The same file was served correctly after a restart.

choices.text: It reads `public/` when it starts, and answers unknown addresses with `index.html`
choices.why: Right. Restart it and the file is there.

choices.text: `curl` asks for HTML unless you tell it you want JSON
choices.why: The server decides by the path, and the path was the same both times.

choices.text: Files in `public/` are only served by `ng build`
choices.why: Both commands copy `public/`; the dev server only needed a restart.

prompt: After you saved `app.html`, the dev server printed `Component update sent to client(s)`. What happened in the open page?

choices.text: It reloaded from the start, losing whatever state it had
choices.why: The point of the message is that it did not reload.

choices.text: Nothing until you pressed F5
choices.why: The update reaches the page on its own, over the dev server's connection.

choices.text: It swapped the new template in place, without a reload
choices.why: Right. Only the changed component was rebuilt and sent.

choices.text: It showed a banner asking you to accept the change
choices.why: There is no banner; the change simply appears.

prompt: `ps` listed the dev server's resident memory in kilobytes. Rounded to the nearest hundred megabytes, how many megabytes is that?
Why does `look` print `[vite] connecting...` against the dev server, and not against the built files?

choices.text: Vite is the production web server, and the dev server imitates it
choices.why: It is the other way round: Vite is what the dev server is built on.

choices.text: `look` connects to Vite to read the page's text
choices.why: `look` reads the page through Chromium; the message is the page's own console.

choices.text: It is the dev server's live-reload connection, which a production build does not have
choices.why: Right. The production build also drops the development-mode message.

choices.text: The production build prints it too, but only after the first click
choices.why: The production build printed nothing to the console at all.

prompt: `npx ng generate component week-summary` wrote a class. What is it called?

choices.text: `WeekSummaryComponent`
choices.why: That is the older naming, from the 2016 style guide. This project uses the newer one.

choices.text: `WeekSummary`
choices.why: Right. Its selector is `app-week-summary` and its files are `week-summary.*`.

choices.text: `AppWeekSummary`
choices.why: The `app` prefix goes on the selector, not on the class.

choices.text: `week-summary`
choices.why: That is the file and folder name; a class name cannot contain a hyphen.

prompt: Why does every selector the CLI generates start with `app-`?

choices.text: Browsers only render custom elements whose names start with `app-`
choices.why: A custom element needs a hyphen somewhere; the prefix is Angular's convention, set by `ng new`.

choices.text: To avoid collisions with other elements
choices.why: Right. It is the project's prefix, chosen when the project was created.

choices.text: Because `app` is the name of the root component
choices.why: The root is `App`, and the prefix would be `app` whatever it was called.

choices.text: It marks the component as standalone
choices.why: Standalone is a property of the decorator, and has nothing to do with the selector.

prompt: To see the files a schematic would write without writing them, add the option `--___`.
The production build named its script `main-J4WVDBNH.js`. What decides the eight characters after `main-`?

choices.text: The build's date and time, so two builds never share a name
choices.why: Two builds of the same code get the same name.

choices.text: A random value chosen at each build, to defeat caches
choices.why: Nothing random: the name has to be reproducible for caching to work.

choices.text: The file's own bytes
choices.why: Right. Change one line and the name changes, so a cached old file is never mistaken for the new one.

choices.text: The version in `package.json`, encoded
choices.why: Every build of version 0.0.0 would then share a name.

prompt: Python's server sent its 404 page for `/courses/git`. What has a host for an Angular application to do with such an address?

choices.text: Redirect it to `/`, so the application starts at its first screen
choices.why: The application would then never see the address the person asked for.

choices.text: Return 404, as it does, and let the browser retry
choices.why: A browser does not retry a 404, and the application never loads.

choices.text: Build one file per address in advance, which `ng build` cannot do
choices.why: Serving `index.html` is enough; lesson 23's prerendering is a different matter.

choices.text: Answer it with `index.html` and let the code route it
choices.why: Right. The dev server already does this, and every hosting service has a setting for it.

prompt: How many kilobytes did the production build estimate would cross the network for the planner's initial files?
An `initial` budget has `maximumWarning: '500kB'` and `maximumError: '1MB'`. The initial files reach 700 kB. What happens?

choices.text: The build succeeds and warns
choices.why: Right. It is past the warning and under the error.

choices.text: The build fails, because 700 kB is over the first limit
choices.why: Only `maximumError` fails a build.

choices.text: Nothing, because budgets are only checked by `ng serve`
choices.why: Budgets belong to the production build configuration.

choices.text: The CLI splits the file in two to stay under 500 kB
choices.why: The CLI reports sizes; it does not rearrange your code to meet them.

prompt: The test `should render title` failed with `Expected: "Hello, planner"` and `Received: "Study planner"`. Which was wrong?

choices.text: The template, which should have kept the welcome heading
choices.why: The heading was changed on purpose; the test was describing the old page.

choices.text: The test, which still expected the page `ng new` wrote
choices.why: Right. A failing test is a disagreement, and here the page was the intended side.

choices.text: jsdom, which cannot read headings
choices.why: jsdom read the heading; the value it received is in the report.

choices.text: Vitest, because `toContain` does not work on text
choices.why: `toContain` works on strings; it compared and found a difference.

prompt: Why do the transcripts run `ng test --watch=false`?

choices.text: Watch mode only works in a desktop browser
choices.why: Watch mode works anywhere; it just never finishes.

choices.text: So the command finishes, which a transcript needs
choices.why: Right. While you work, leaving it watching is the useful way.

choices.text: Because watching skips the tests that failed before
choices.why: Watching reruns affected tests; it skips nothing.

choices.text: Without it, `ng test` runs the dev server instead
choices.why: It runs the tests either way; the flag only decides whether it stays.

prompt: `ng update @angular/core@22 @angular/cli@22` first answered `Repository is not clean`. Why does it insist on a clean repository?

choices.text: Because it pushes to the remote after updating
choices.why: It never pushes anything.

choices.text: Because uncommitted files would be deleted by the update
choices.why: It deletes nothing; it edits.

choices.text: So the next diff shows only the migrations
choices.why: Right. You can then read exactly what the update changed.

choices.text: Git is how it downloads the new version
choices.why: The packages come from the npm registry.

prompt: Put what happens, when you run `ng update @angular/core@22 @angular/cli@22` on a clean repository with a new enough Node, in order.
items: it checks that the repository has no uncommitted changes
it installs a temporary copy of the version 22 CLI
that copy checks the version of Node
the packages move to 22 and the migrations edit your code

prompt: Your team wants Angular 22. According to this lesson, where is the first change made?

choices.text: In `package.json`, by editing the versions by hand to 22
choices.why: Hand-edited versions skip the migrations, and the CLI 22 would still refuse the Node.

choices.text: In the track's Node, which must reach 22.22.3
choices.why: Right. The CLI refuses before it changes anything, so the project cannot move first.

choices.text: In `angular.json`, whose builder names carry the version
choices.why: The builders are named without a version.

choices.text: In `.npmrc`, by removing `legacy-peer-deps`
choices.why: That setting is about npm's defect, not about Angular's version.

prompt: Which of these files belong in the planner's git repository? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `package-lock.json`
choices.why: Right. It is what `npm ci` rebuilds from.

choices.text: `.npmrc`
choices.why: Right. Without it, the next `npm install` crashes again.

choices.text: `node_modules/`
choices.why: It can always be rebuilt, and `.gitignore` leaves it out.

choices.text: `dist/`
choices.why: Build output is made again from the source; `.gitignore` leaves it out.

choices.text: `public/courses.json`
choices.why: Right. It is source: the planner's data.

prompt: You want to know whether your change broke anything, and then see it in a browser. Which pair of commands, in which order?

choices.text: `ng build`, then `ng update`
choices.why: Neither tells you whether the behaviour broke, and `ng update` changes versions.

choices.text: `ng generate`, then `ng serve`
choices.why: `ng generate` writes new files; it checks nothing.

choices.text: `ng test`, then `ng serve`
choices.why: Right. The tests answer the first question, and the dev server the second.

choices.text: `ng serve`, then `ng new`
choices.why: `ng new` starts a different project.
